name: Sverre Fehn
bio: Fehn graduated in Oslo in 1949, joined the Norwegian CIAM offshoot PAGON, travelled Morocco to study primitive building, and spent a year in Jean Prouvé's Paris orbit — then went home and stayed. The Brussels pavilion of 1958 and the Nordic Pavilion in Venice made his name by doing almost nothing: a few concrete beams calibrated to turn southern sun into shadowless northern light. At the bishop's barn in Hamar he ran laminated ramps and vitrines over medieval ruins, insisting that 'only by manifestation of the present can we make the past speak.' He built little — mostly museums and houses in Norway — taught at the Oslo School of Architecture for a quarter century, and waited. The Pritzker arrived in 1997, roughly thirty years after the work that earned it.

projects.title: Hedmark Museum
projects.blurb: Concrete ramps and timber vitrines threaded through a medieval bishop's barn — the past made to speak by the present, not restored by it.

projects.title: Nordic Pavilion
projects.blurb: Two crossed layers of slender concrete beams sieve the Venetian sun into even northern light; the site's trees grow on through the roof.

projects.title: Norwegian Glacier Museum
projects.blurb: A concrete instrument for looking at ice, set on the flat valley floor beneath the Jostedal glacier with stairs that climb to the view.

projects.title: Villa Busk
projects.blurb: A house laid along a rock ridge like a bridge, ending in a tower reached by a timber walkway; his most complete late house.

projects.title: Norwegian Pavilion, Expo 58
projects.blurb: The competition win that launched him at thirty-three — a light, precise box that read as Norwegian without a single folk motif.

projects.title: Ivar Aasen Centre
projects.blurb: A museum for the creator of the Nynorsk written language, cut as a long curved section into the hillside of his birthplace.

projects.title: Aukrust Centre
projects.blurb: One long laminated-timber and concrete beam of a building beneath the mountains, housing the cartoonist Kjell Aukrust's universe.

projects.title: Villa Norrköping
projects.blurb: A competition-won house on a square plan whose rooms pinwheel around a top-lit core — Fehn's domestic ideas at their clearest.

projects.title: Schreiner House
projects.blurb: A brick and timber house for a professor of anatomy, organized around the ritual of a tree in the courtyard.

projects.title: National Museum – Architecture
projects.blurb: His last work: a glass exhibition pavilion braced by sculptural concrete, added behind Grosch's 1830 bank building.

name: Robert Venturi & Denise Scott Brown
bio: Venturi's Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture (1966) answered Mies with 'less is a bore' and rehabilitated the ambiguous, the ordinary and the both-and; Scott Brown, a Zambian-born planner trained in London, brought the social sciences and the American strip. Together — married in 1967, partners in Learning from Las Vegas in 1972 — they taught architects to distinguish the duck from the decorated shed and to look at billboards without sneering. The gabled house Venturi built for his mother in Chestnut Hill fired the opening shot of postmodernism at exactly domestic scale. Their buildings, from Guild House to the Sainsbury Wing, are deadpan, allusive and more radical than they look. The 1991 Pritzker went to Venturi alone; Scott Brown declined to attend, and a 2013 petition demanding her retroactive inclusion gathered twenty thousand signatures but no medal.

projects.title: Vanna Venturi House
projects.blurb: The house Venturi built for his mother: a split gable, an off-center chimney and a stair to nowhere — complexity and contradiction demonstrated in five rooms.

projects.title: Sainsbury Wing, National Gallery
projects.blurb: The extension that ended the 'monstrous carbuncle' saga — Corinthian pilasters syncopating away from Wilkins's facade, and top-lit rooms that flatter early Renaissance altarpieces.

projects.title: Guild House
projects.blurb: Housing for the elderly in ordinary dark brick with a giant entrance column and, originally, a gold anodized TV antenna as crowning ornament.

projects.title: Franklin Court
projects.blurb: Benjamin Franklin's vanished house evoked as a white steel ghost frame over an underground museum — memory built without fakery.

projects.title: Gordon Wu Hall
projects.blurb: A dining and social hall spliced into Princeton's collegiate Gothic, announced by a flattened marble-and-granite heraldic entrance.

projects.title: Seattle Art Museum
projects.blurb: A limestone-and-terracotta downtown museum with a grand stair climbing the hillside inside; Hammering Man swings his arm out front.

projects.title: Allen Memorial Art Museum Addition
projects.blurb: A checkerboard granite-and-sandstone loft grafted onto Cass Gilbert's museum, with one ironic Ionic column in the crack between old and new.

projects.title: Fire Station No. 4
projects.blurb: A firehouse in Columbus, Indiana rendered as a decorated shed — white brick, red doors and an outsized numeral doing the architecture.

projects.title: Lieb House
projects.blurb: A shore cottage with asbestos shingles and a giant number 9; in 2009 it was barged up the Atlantic coast to a new site rather than be demolished.

projects.title: Trubek and Wislocki Houses
projects.blurb: Two plain shingled cottages angled toward each other above the water — vernacular deployed with total knowingness, endlessly imitated since.

name: Frei Otto
bio: Otto — the first name means 'free'; his stonemason father was making a point — flew gliders as a boy, was drafted as a Luftwaffe pilot, and spent two years in a French POW camp engineering shelter for thousands out of almost nothing. The lesson became a career: his 1954 doctorate on suspended roofs, tested with soap films, hanging chains and stocking fabric, founded the modern discipline of lightweight structure. The cable-net German Pavilion at Expo 67 and the acrylic clouds over the 1972 Munich Olympics gave a democratic Germany an architecture pointedly opposite to Speer's granite. From his Institute for Lightweight Structures at Stuttgart — itself a tent — he pursued minimal material for maximum span, decades before sustainability had a name. He died in March 2015, one day before the announcement that he had won the Pritzker.

projects.title: Munich Olympic Stadium Roofs
projects.blurb: With Günter Behnisch: acrylic clouds on cable nets sweeping over stadium, arena and pool — a deliberately weightless answer to the Berlin of 1936.

projects.title: German Pavilion, Expo 67
projects.blurb: With Rolf Gutbrod: a floating cable-net landscape prototyped at full scale in Stuttgart — the building that exported German lightness to the world.

projects.title: Multihalle
projects.blurb: The world's largest self-supporting timber gridshell, form-found with a hanging chain-net model and still standing on slender laths.

projects.title: Institute for Lightweight Structures
projects.blurb: His university laboratory, built as the test rig for the Montreal pavilion and kept as a working tent for four decades of research.

projects.title: Tuwaiq Palace
projects.blurb: With Gutbrod and Buro Happold: a fortress wall snaking along a desert escarpment, with white tensile tents blooming from its flanks.

projects.title: Tanzbrunnen Tent
projects.blurb: A star-wave canopy over a dance fountain at the federal garden show — an early membrane roof charming enough to be kept permanently.

projects.title: Hellabrunn Aviary
projects.blurb: A cable-net mesh draped over the zoo's birds, so minimal it reads as a shimmer above the trees.

projects.title: Japan Pavilion, Expo 2000
projects.blurb: With Shigeru Ban: a gridshell of recyclable paper tubes — the old master consulting on the lightest structure of the fair.

projects.title: Ökohaus
projects.blurb: IBA eco-housing conceived as concrete tree-frames into which residents built their own dwellings among the foliage.

projects.title: Bundesgartenschau Music Pavilion
projects.blurb: His first built membrane: a four-point saddle tent over a garden-show bandstand, erected in days and remembered for decades.

name: James Stirling
firm: James Stirling Michael Wilford and Associates
bio: A marine engineer's son raised in Liverpool, Stirling jumped into Normandy as a paratrooper, was twice wounded, and came home to study architecture in a city of docks and grand Victorian machinery he never stopped quoting. With James Gowan he built the Leicester Engineering Building — red tile, patent glazing, forms following programme with alarming glee — and then, alone, the glass-cascade History Faculty at Cambridge and the Florey Building at Oxford, a 'red trilogy' as admired as it leaked. In the seventies the work swerved through neoclassicism toward the Neue Staatsgalerie in Stuttgart, where a marble-banded ruin, a public ramp and lime-green mullions made postmodernism briefly look profound. He won the Pritzker in 1981 and died in 1992, at sixty-six, of complications after routine surgery. Britain named its highest architecture prize after a man whose buildings it had repeatedly tried to demolish.

projects.title: Neue Staatsgalerie
projects.blurb: A sandstone-and-travertine museum wrapped around an open rotunda, crossed by a public ramp and punctuated by lime-green glazing — postmodernism's most convincing public building.

projects.title: Engineering Building, University of Leicester
projects.blurb: With James Gowan: crystalline workshop glazing, cantilevered lecture theatres and red tile towers — programme turned directly into form.

projects.title: History Faculty Building
projects.blurb: A tent of glass cascading over a fan-shaped reading room; chronically troublesome, once nearly demolished by university vote, never forgotten.

projects.title: Florey Building
projects.blurb: Queen's College student rooms banked in a red glazed horseshoe facing the river — the last and strangest panel of the red trilogy.

projects.title: No 1 Poultry
projects.blurb: A striped pink-and-yellow prow in the heart of the City, built after his death and now the youngest Grade II* listed building in England.

projects.title: Clore Gallery
projects.blurb: The Turner wing at the Tate: a garden pavilion whose grid quietly changes material as it approaches its neoclassical neighbour.

projects.title: Arthur M. Sackler Museum
projects.blurb: Harvard's antiquities museum behind a striped polychrome facade, with a monumental stair squeezed to theatrical effect.

projects.title: Wissenschaftszentrum Berlin
projects.blurb: A social science institute disassembled into a pink-and-blue city of primitive building types — theatre, campanile, stoa — around a garden.

projects.title: Langham House Close
projects.blurb: With Gowan: brick-and-concrete flats near Ham Common whose exposed aggregate and gaskets helped define the New Brutalism at domestic scale.

projects.title: Olivetti Training Centre
projects.blurb: Glass-reinforced polyester wings in period-perfect seventies mauve, clipped onto an Edwardian country house for typewriter salesmen.

name: Balkrishna Doshi
bio: Born in Pune to a family of furniture makers, Doshi studied in Bombay, sailed for London, and talked his way into Le Corbusier's Paris atelier in 1951 — working the first months unpaid — before returning to supervise the master's buildings in Ahmedabad and Chandigarh. He later brought Louis Kahn to Ahmedabad for the Indian Institute of Management, absorbed both giants, and spent the next six decades translating their concrete into something Indian: shaded, porous, incremental, alive to ritual and monsoon. His practice Vastushilpa, founded in 1956, ran from Sangath, a studio of sunken mosaic-clad vaults he called an extension of his own memory. Aranya in Indore housed the poor with plots, plinths and services rather than finished flats, trusting families to build the rest. He founded the school that became CEPT University, taught there for decades, and in 2018 became the first Indian architect to win the Pritzker.

projects.title: Sangath
projects.blurb: His own studio: sunken barrel vaults sheathed in broken china mosaic, water channels and grassy amphitheatre steps — an office built like a memory palace.

projects.title: Aranya Low Cost Housing
projects.blurb: Sites-and-services housing for eighty thousand people — plinths, cores and demonstration houses that families extend themselves; Aga Khan Award, 1995.

projects.title: Indian Institute of Management Bangalore
projects.blurb: A campus of grey granite corridors open to sky and creeper — Fatehpur Sikri's labyrinth reworked for management studies.

projects.title: CEPT University Campus
projects.blurb: The architecture school he founded: parallel brick-and-concrete studio lofts, open on all sides, where the section itself teaches.

projects.title: Amdavad ni Gufa
projects.blurb: An underground gallery for M. F. Husain's murals beneath ferrocement turtle-shell domes tiled in china mosaic — architecture and painting as one creature.

projects.title: Institute of Indology
projects.blurb: An early concrete frame raised on a plinth for ancient manuscripts, balancing Corbusian section against traditional verandah depth.

projects.title: Tagore Memorial Hall
projects.blurb: A 700-seat theatre held in folded concrete plates — Doshi's most overtly Brutalist public building.

projects.title: Premabhai Hall
projects.blurb: A raw concrete theatre lifted above the old city, its foyer terraces conceived as an extension of the street.

projects.title: Kamala House
projects.blurb: His own house, named for his wife: brick cavity walls, a pinwheel plan and fierce climatic economy on a modest budget.

projects.title: Life Insurance Corporation Housing
projects.blurb: Stepped duplex terraces mixing three income groups in one section, each roof a future floor for the family below.

name: Gae Aulenti
bio: Gaetana Aulenti graduated from Milan Polytechnic in 1953, one of two women in a class of twenty, and joined the circle around Ernesto Rogers at Casabella-Continuità, where the young Milanese were busy scandalizing orthodox modernists with Neo-Liberty curves. For two decades she was better known for interiors, exhibitions, stage sets for Luca Ronconi and objects — the 1965 Pipistrello lamp, designed for Olivetti's Paris showroom, still sells. Then the Gare d'Orsay: her 1980–86 conversion of the Beaux-Arts station into the Musée d'Orsay, monumental stone galleries inserted under Laloux's vault, was attacked by critics and embraced by the public, and made her the age's specialist in putting museums inside monuments. Pompidou's galleries, Palazzo Grassi, Barcelona's national museum and San Francisco's Asian Art Museum followed. Milan named the piazza at the foot of its new towers after her within weeks of her death.

projects.title: Musée d'Orsay
projects.blurb: The Beaux-Arts railway station remade as the museum of the nineteenth century — stone gallery-buildings marching down the nave under Laloux's iron vault.

projects.title: Palazzo Grassi
projects.blurb: The last palace on the Grand Canal turned into Fiat's exhibition machine — discreet servicing, luminous rooms, blockbuster shows.

projects.title: Musée National d'Art Moderne, Centre Pompidou
projects.blurb: Proper rooms and enfilades reinstated inside Piano and Rogers's open floors — a polemical correction the curators had begged for.

projects.title: Museu Nacional d'Art de Catalunya
projects.blurb: The vast 1929 exhibition palace on Montjuïc reorganized over two decades into Catalonia's national museum, its oval hall kept as civic interior.

projects.title: Asian Art Museum
projects.blurb: The old Beaux-Arts public library across from City Hall opened up around a skylit court for one of the largest Asian collections outside Asia.

projects.title: Scuderie del Quirinale
projects.blurb: The papal stables on the Quirinal hill converted into Rome's premier exhibition halls, with a glazed stair overlooking the city.

projects.title: Palavela
projects.blurb: The 1961 concrete sail re-skinned with a crisp inner building for Olympic figure skating — one Italian monument nested in another.

projects.title: Piazzale Cadorna
projects.blurb: Station front and square redesigned as a piece of urban theatre, with Oldenburg and van Bruggen's giant needle and thread as punctuation.

projects.title: Istituto Italiano di Cultura
projects.blurb: Italy's cultural institute as a sheer slab in saturated red — a color argument conducted at urban scale, to local controversy.

projects.title: Olivetti Showroom
projects.blurb: A spiraling showroom-as-stage for typewriters on Rue du Faubourg Saint-Honoré, for which the Pipistrello lamp was designed.

name: Fumihiko Maki
bio: Maki studied under Tange in Tokyo, then at Cranbrook and Harvard, worked for SOM and Sert, and taught in St. Louis — the most cosmopolitan formation of any Japanese architect of his generation. The youngest signatory of the 1960 Metabolist manifesto, he was also its quietest: his Investigations in Collective Form argued for 'group form,' cities growing by linked increments rather than megastructural machines. He proved it over twenty-five years at Hillside Terrace in Tokyo, a low-rise quarter built phase by patient phase along one Daikanyama street. His buildings — Spiral, the Tokyo Metropolitan Gymnasium, 4 World Trade Center — favor aluminum, glass and stainless steel handled with an almost ethical restraint. He won the Pritzker in 1993 and kept the office producing lucid work until his death in 2024 at ninety-five.

projects.title: Hillside Terrace
projects.blurb: A quarter century of low-rise phases along one Daikanyama street — 'group form' proven as patient, livable urbanism rather than manifesto.

projects.title: Spiral
projects.blurb: An Aoyama arts building whose collaged facade and eponymous ramped atrium mix gallery, café and commerce into one cultured machine.

projects.title: Tokyo Metropolitan Gymnasium
projects.blurb: A stainless-clad arena sunk into its site beneath a great segmented shell — monumental span worn lightly.

projects.title: Fujisawa Municipal Gymnasium
projects.blurb: Paired stainless-steel roofs like a samurai helmet seen from afar; Maki's metallic craft at its most sculptural.

projects.title: Makuhari Messe
projects.blurb: A convention center of enormous arced roofs outside Tokyo — infrastructure-scale building kept legible and calm.

projects.title: 4 World Trade Center
projects.blurb: The quietest tower on the rebuilt site: a minimalist glass shaft that dissolves into sky, by deliberate deference to the memorial.

projects.title: Aga Khan Museum
projects.blurb: A white granite museum for Islamic art angled around a courtyard of light — precision standing in for ornament.

projects.title: Kaze-no-Oka Crematorium
projects.blurb: Brick, concrete and weathering steel volumes set among burial mounds — a landscape for grief, widely considered his most moving work.

projects.title: MIT Media Lab
projects.blurb: A glass-veiled matrix of double-height labs around a central atrium, engineered for the collisions the Lab is famous for.

projects.title: National Museum of Modern Art, Kyoto
projects.blurb: A gridded, courteous museum facing the Heian Shrine gate — modernism calibrated to a historic district's manners.
projects.wikipedia: National Museum of Modern Art, Kyoto

name: Paulo Mendes da Rocha
bio: An engineer's son from Vitória, Mendes da Rocha won the Paulistano gymnasium competition at twenty-nine — a steel ring floated on six concrete blades — and spent the next six decades refining that one heroic idea: maximum span, minimum touch, public ground flowing underneath. With Vilanova Artigas he defined the Paulista school, rougher and more structural than Rio's curves; the military dictatorship stripped both of their teaching posts at USP in 1969, and he was not reinstated until democracy returned. Nearly everything he built stands in São Paulo, a city he loved as pure artifact — his own Casa Butantã, the buried MuBE, the levitating canopy of Praça do Patriarca. He worked from a small office with a drawing board and no computer. The Pritzker came in 2006, the Venice Golden Lion and RIBA Gold Medal in his final decade, changing his habits not at all.

projects.title: Brazilian Museum of Sculpture
projects.blurb: A museum that is mostly plaza: galleries buried below ground, with a sixty-meter prestressed concrete beam as the only building visible.

projects.title: Paulistano Athletic Club Gymnasium
projects.blurb: Won at twenty-nine: a steel compression ring hung from six raw concrete blades, with the arena open to the air beneath.

projects.title: Pinacoteca do Estado Renovation
projects.blurb: The unfinished nineteenth-century museum crossed with steel walkways over its courtyards — restoration as frank modern intervention.
projects.wikipedia: Pinacoteca do Estado de São Paulo

projects.title: Brazilian Pavilion, Expo 70
projects.blurb: A flat concrete roof hovering over an artificial undulating ground, nearly wall-less — Brazil represented by structure and topography alone.

projects.title: Casa Butantã
projects.blurb: His own house: a raw concrete table on four supports, bedrooms lit from above, domesticity treated as an engineering problem with tenderness.

projects.title: Praça do Patriarca Canopy
projects.blurb: A white steel portico suspended from a single arc over the entrance to the underground city — infrastructure turned civic gesture.

projects.title: Chapel of Saint Peter
projects.blurb: A tiny chapel beside a governor's palace: one concrete column, glass, and a suspended slab doing the work of a nave.

projects.title: Serra Dourada Stadium
projects.blurb: A state stadium under one enormous open concrete roof, its terraces continuous with the ground of the cerrado.

projects.title: SESC 24 de Maio
projects.blurb: With MMBB: a downtown department store hollowed into a vertical leisure center, ramps spiraling up to a rooftop public pool.

projects.title: National Coach Museum
projects.blurb: His major work outside Brazil: gilded royal carriages displayed in a great elevated concrete hall over an open public ground floor.

name: Frank Gehry
bio: Born Frank Goldberg in Toronto, where his grandmother built him cities from wood scraps off the hardware-store floor, Gehry moved to Los Angeles at seventeen, drove a delivery truck through USC, and practiced conventionally until 1978 — when he wrapped his own Santa Monica bungalow in chain-link, plywood and corrugated metal and detonated his career. He befriended painters and sculptors rather than architects, and got his crumpled forms built by borrowing CATIA from the aerospace industry, making the office a pioneer of digital fabrication. The Guggenheim Bilbao of 1997 turned a rusting port city into a pilgrimage site and gave urban policy a new noun, the Bilbao effect. Disney Hall, Fondation Louis Vuitton and the Luma tower in Arles followed, each accused of spectacle and each vindicated by use. He won the Pritzker in 1989, kept working past ninety-five, and died in Santa Monica in December 2025, aged ninety-six.

projects.title: Guggenheim Museum Bilbao
projects.blurb: Titanium sails billowing along the Nervión — the museum that revived a rusting port city and lent its name to an entire urban strategy.

projects.title: Walt Disney Concert Hall
projects.blurb: Stainless-steel curves around a superb Toyota-tuned vineyard hall — sixteen years from sketch to opening night, and worth the wait acoustically.

projects.title: Gehry Residence
projects.blurb: A pink Dutch colonial bungalow wrapped in chain-link, plywood and corrugated metal — the cheap-materials manifesto that started everything.

projects.title: Fondation Louis Vuitton
projects.blurb: Twelve glass sails rigged over white gallery blocks in the Bois de Boulogne — his most technically extravagant building.

projects.title: Dancing House
projects.blurb: With Vlado Milunić: 'Fred and Ginger' swaying on a riverside corner, post-communist Prague's argument about what new buildings may do.

projects.title: Vitra Design Museum
projects.blurb: His first European building: white plaster volumes tumbling on the Vitra campus, deconstructivism at garden scale.

projects.title: Ray and Maria Stata Center
projects.blurb: MIT's computer science labs as a colliding village of tilted towers — beloved, leak-prone, and litigated by its own client.

projects.title: 8 Spruce Street
projects.blurb: A 76-story rippling stainless residential tower by City Hall — his proof that the crumpled surface could go fully vertical.

projects.title: Weisman Art Museum
projects.blurb: A brushed-steel cliff of curves above the Mississippi at the University of Minnesota — Bilbao's ideas at rehearsal scale.

projects.title: Luma Arles
projects.blurb: A twisting tower of 11,000 stainless panels rising from a Roman town's railyards — the late-career work critics argued about most.

name: Charles Correa
bio: Born in Secunderabad and trained at Michigan and MIT, Correa opened his Bombay office in 1958 and announced himself with the Gandhi memorial museum at Sabarmati — a village of tiled pavilions humble enough for its subject. His shorthand was 'form follows climate': open-to-sky courts, verandahs, and section as shading device, worked out in everything from luxury towers to the incremental Belapur housing where each poor family got ground, sky and room to build. As chief architect of Navi Mumbai he planned a new city for two million across the harbor, and he chaired India's National Commission on Urbanisation, insisting the city was a resource, not a problem. Late works like Jawahar Kala Kendra and the Bhopal assembly organized modern programmes on cosmological mandalas without a whiff of kitsch. The RIBA gave him its Gold Medal in 1984 and, on his death in 2015, called him India's greatest architect.

projects.title: Gandhi Smarak Sangrahalaya
projects.blurb: The Gandhi memorial museum at Sabarmati Ashram: a modular village of brick piers, tiled roofs and water courts, monumental by refusing monumentality.

projects.title: Jawahar Kala Kendra
projects.blurb: An arts center planned as the nine-square navagraha mandala of Jaipur itself, one square slid aside — cosmology as working floor plan.

projects.title: Kanchanjunga Apartments
projects.blurb: A 28-story tower of interlocking double-height apartments whose cut-away corner terraces are climate section made luxury housing.

projects.title: Bharat Bhavan
projects.blurb: A multi-arts complex terraced down to Bhopal's lake as sunken courts and gardens — a cultural building you walk over as much as into.

projects.title: Vidhan Bhavan
projects.blurb: Madhya Pradesh's state assembly as a circular citadel of courts and chambers on a mandala plan; Aga Khan Award, 1998.

projects.title: Champalimaud Centre for the Unknown
projects.blurb: His last major work: a biomedical research campus in curved stone facing the Atlantic, a ceremonial axis running to the water.

projects.title: Belapur Incremental Housing
projects.blurb: Low-rise, high-density housing where every family owns ground and open sky and can extend the house themselves — his housing arguments built.

projects.title: British Council Headquarters
projects.blurb: A layered facade telling India's history of encounters, fronted by a giant Howard Hodgkin banyan-shadow mural in marble and granite.

projects.title: Ismaili Centre
projects.blurb: A prayer hall under a crystalline glass dome, paired with Maki's Aga Khan Museum across a formal garden.

projects.title: Jeevan Bharati
projects.blurb: The Life Insurance Corporation's mirrored megastructure on Connaught Place, framing the colonial circus through a giant public portal.
